newsitem.title: USA: IPO VIEW - Prospects improved, liquidity still key.
newsitem.headline: IPO VIEW - Prospects improved, liquidity still key.

text.p: Prospects for initial public offerings of high-tech firms are brighter after the red-hot debuts of Rambus Inc. and Internet bookseller Amazon.com set off fireworks on Wall Street.

But IPO analysts warn the cloud hanging over the market recently has yet to lift. Buyers, especially mutual fund managers scorched by weak returns, remain very choosy and favor large deals that offer the safety of liquidity.
"You can't turn an ocean liner around on a dime. A few hot deals do not indicate a quick turnaround," said David Menlow, president of the IPO Financial Network.
The predilection for blue chip issues with prestigious underwriters means strong demand for Hartford Life Inc.'s $586.5 million IPO this week.
John Fitzgibbon, editor of the IPO Aftermarket, estimates the deal could jump $2 to $4 a share at its debut.
"It's an institutional sweetheart," said Menlow. Goldman Sachs is the lead underwriter of the stock offering of the unit of ITT Hartford Financial Services Group Inc..

IPOs of high tech firms could get a badly needed lift from the buzz created by the two explosive IPOs last week -- Rambus vaulted 150 percent on its first day to $30.25 from its IPO price of $12. Its technology speeds the processing capability of semiconductor chips up to four times. The stock closed the week even higher, at $31.75.

Seattle bookseller Amazon.com surged as high as 66 percent at its Nasdaq market debut. But concerns about future profitability and competition led some investors to take quick profits. The stock closed Friday at $20.75, with a much slimmer gain of 15 percent from its IPO price of $18.
No IPOs on deck this week are forecast to repeat last week's sensations, according to analysts.
"I was really surprised by those deals. Most investors are very cautious and I don't think that's going to change any time soon," said Margarita Perez, president of Fortaleza Asset Management.
She said few upcoming IPOs were drawing her firm's interest, although she was planning to take a close look at Polo Ralph Lauren. The designer is aiming to raise $600 million in a June IPO.

Menlow said any recovering in the IPO market is not likely to follow the neat "V" chart pattern of the broader market, which recovered quickly after falling nearly 10 percent from highs set in early March.

A trim pipeline of 313 IPOs and secondary offerings could also help. In a Darwinian twist on the new issues market, many slated IPOs were postponed or cancelled in an April drought in new issues, the worst month in more than two years. The hardy crop of companies that survived have been able to show promise early in the IPO process.

Other IPOs forecast to reap small premiums this week by Fitzgibbon are Healthcare Recoveries Inc., a $137.2 million IPO from Bear Stearns. The company provides healthcare subrogation and related recovery services. The deal could rise 75 cents or more in the aftermarket.
Similar gains could come from Lexington Healthcare Group Inc., a provider of long-term subacute care coming from underwriter Mason Hill.

Also going public this week are Cardima Inc., which makes microcatheters that treat abnormal heart rhythms and real estate investment trust Alexandria Real Estate of Pasadena, California. Alexandria will offer 6.75 million shares for between $20 to $22 each in an offering by PaineWebber Inc.
